title: Reporting kutob can save children from online sexual abuse, exploitation, says NGO
summary: Authorities are encouraging people to report even a suspicion that something is wrong or kutob in cases related to online sexual abuse or exploitation of children (OSAEC).

blocks.text: Authorities are encouraging people to report even a suspicion that something is wrong or kutob in cases related to online sexual abuse or exploitation of children (OSAEC).

“Protecting a child begins with something as simple as a kutob, a feeling that something is not right,” said International Justice Mission (IJM) Philippines Community Engagement Director Evelyn Pingul in a statement.

“We don’t need to have proof of abuse before reporting our concerns. Through this campaign, we want to encourage every Filipino to recognize the warning signs, speak up, and take action. One report could make all the difference in a child’s life,” she added.
The IJM said that OSAEC often takes place within the home and is a "pervasive yet underreported crime that is too often dismissed as a private family matter."
A study conducted by IJM Philippines and the University of Nottingham’s Rights Lab showed that one in every 100 Filipino children experienced OSAEC in 2022 alone.
"Children affected by OSAEC may exhibit warning signs such as chronic fatigue from possible late-night livestreaming sessions, social withdrawal due to trauma, or visible distress," the group said.

"Household indicators may also suggest exploitation, including frequent visits to money remittance centers despite having no known family ties abroad, unexplained improvements in lifestyle, or the presence of multiple gadgets and internet-enabled devices without a clear purpose."

Department of Justice Assistant Secretary Michelle Anne Lapuz, in the same statement, encouraged Filipinos to call the DOJ-Inter-Agency Council Against Trafficking 1343 Actionline if they notice OSAEC red flags or have information that could help law enforcement initiate an investigation.
“The Philippine government has functional helplines staffed by operators equipped to handle reports of possible OSAEC incidents,” said Lapuz, who leads IACAT.

“Remaining silent despite having kutob or suspicion that a child is being sexually abused and exploited online only enables traffickers to continue their crimes and inflict further trauma on their victims,” she added.

As part of “May Kutob? Mag-Report” campaign, which aims to encourage Filipinos to report suspected OSAEC cases, the IJM and the DOJ-IACAT organized the five-kilometer community run held on Sunday in Ortigas East, Pasig City.
The activity was also supported by Women’s Run PH, the Pasig City Government, the Pasig City Police Office, and the Philippine National Police – Women and Children Protection Center.

Meanwhile, Ambassador Roderick Wols of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Philippines led the ceremonial send-off of the runners. There were also Dutch participants, who are in the country for Muskathlon, a separate endurance event that also supports efforts to combat OSAEC. — BAP, GMA News
